title: Yitzhak Rabin
wiki_lead:
Yitzhak Rabin (; Hebrew: יִצְחָק רַבִּין, IPA: [itsˈχak ˈʁabin]; 1 March 1922 – 4 November 1995) was an Israeli statesman and general who was the prime minister of Israel, having served from 1974 to 1977 and again from 1992 until his assassination in 1995. He was the first prime minister to have been born in the region of Palestine, at the time under British control.
Rabin was born in Jerusalem to Jewish immigrants from Eastern Europe and was raised in a Labor Zionist household. He learned agriculture in school and excelled as a student. As a teenager, he joined the Palmach, the commando force of the Yishuv. He eventually rose through its ranks to become its chief of operations during the 1948 Arab–Israeli War. In late 1948, he joined the newly formed Israel Defense Forces and continued to rise as a promising officer, with a 27-year career as a professional soldier. He ultimately attained the rank of Rav Aluf, the most senior rank in the Israeli Defense Force (often translated as lieutenant general). In the 1950s, Rabin helped shape the training doctrine of the IDF and he led its Operations Directorate from 1959 to 1963. He was appointed chief of the general staff in 1964 and oversaw Israel's victory in the 1967 Six-Day War.
Rabin served as Israel's ambassador to the United States from 1968 to 1973, during a period of deepening U.S.–Israel ties. He was appointed Prime Minister of Israel in 1974 after the resignation of Golda Meir. In his first term, Rabin signed the Sinai Interim Agreement and ordered the Entebbe raid. He resigned in 1977 in the wake of a financial scandal. Rabin was Israel's minister of defense for much of the 1980s, including during the outbreak of the First Intifada.
In 1992, Rabin was re-elected as prime minister on a platform embracing the Israeli–Palestinian peace process. He signed several historic agreements with the Palestinian leadership as part of the Oslo Accords.  In 1994, Rabin won the Nobel Peace Prize together with long-time political rival Shimon Peres and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat. Rabin also signed a peace treaty with Jordan in 1994. In November 1995, he was assassinated by Yigal Amir, an extremist who opposed the terms of the Oslo Accords. Amir was convicted of Rabin's murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. Rabin was the first native-born prime minister of Israel, the only prime minister to be assassinated, and the second to die in office after Levi Eshkol. Rabin has become a symbol of the Israeli–Palestinian peace process.

Family background

grok_lead: Yitzhak Rabin (1 March 1922 â 4 November 1995) was an Israeli general and statesman who commanded the Israel Defense Forces during the 1967 Six-Day War and served as the country's fifth prime minister in two non-consecutive terms, from 1974 to 1977 and from 1992 until his assassination. Born in Jerusalem to parents who had immigrated from Eastern Europe, Rabin received agricultural training before joining the elite Palmach commando unit of the Haganah in 1941, where he participated in operations during the 1948 Arab-Israeli War, including the controversial shelling of the Irgun arms ship Altalena off Tel Aviv, which resulted in fatalities among Jewish fighters and heightened internal divisions. Appointed IDF Chief of the General Staff in 1964, he directed preparations and operations that led to Israel's rapid defeat of Egypt, Jordan, and Syria in 1967, capturing the Sinai Peninsula, Gaza Strip, West Bank, and Golan Heights. Following military service, Rabin served as ambassador to the United States from 1968 to 1973, then entered politics as a Labor Party leader. His initial premiership emphasized security and partial disengagement from Egyptian forces but concluded with his resignation in 1977 over a scandal involving unauthorized foreign bank accounts held by him and his wife, Leah. Returning as prime minister in 1992, Rabin authorized secret negotiations culminating in the 1993 Oslo Accords with the Palestine Liberation Organization, establishing the Palestinian Authority for interim self-governance in parts of the West Bank and Gaza amid hopes for eventual peace, though the process immediately faced criticism for enabling increased terrorist attacks and failing to curb Palestinian rejectionism. These efforts earned him, along with Foreign Minister Shimon Peres and PLO leader Yasser Arafat, the 1994 Nobel Peace Prize, yet provoked intense domestic backlash from opponents who argued the concessions undermined Israel's strategic depth and invited violence. On 4 November 1995, after addressing a Tel Aviv rally supporting the peace initiative, Rabin was shot dead by Yigal Amir, an ultranationalist Jewish law student who viewed the accords as treasonous and a betrayal of biblical claims to the land.
